chapter_theme: The city's women crowd the streets, jewelled, bewildered and shamed, to watch Civakan pass in procession, and in the last verses throw powder and flowers, praise him as Murugan's brother and Kama, and beg him with their eyes.

cast.role: the hero, whom the city's women watch
the women of the city who throng to see Civakan
the young girls among the watchers
the maidens who dress before mirrors

2527.reading: The street is so thick with banner-staffs, perfumed smoke, fine powder and flower-pollen that the birds can no longer tell the time of day and gather in distress.
2527.nuance: The scene opens the crowding of the city around the wedding day; nothing here names who is coming, so it is setting only.

2528.reading: Gems fall from the coin-strings the bangled women have loosed, and a young peahen, taking them for fire or for red velvet mites, shrinks from the ground and pecks at them till the jewels seem to laugh at her.
2528.nuance: The peahen's mistake is the poet's proof of how much jewellery has been scattered: loss of ornament is shown as a bird's confusion, not a woman's grief.

2529.reading: Girls with childish, innocent looks, anklets ringing and gold ear-ornaments slipping as they run, seem Kama himself born as a woman so that his heart could know desire.
2529.nuance: The simile makes the girls the god of love's own experiment: he becomes female in order to feel what his arrows cause.

2530.reading: The budding girls, their pearl-strung young breasts swelling as though Kama himself were growing them, stand hurrying forward, their hair bulging behind, as if set there for show.
2530.event: The young girls of the city press forward to see.

2531.reading: The long evening, with its moonlight, leaves the stage empty; the women, joined by friends with crescent brows, stand bewildered in the jewel-lit dusk like a golden creeper hung with bright gems.
2531.nuance: Mayakkam (bewilderment) here is the desire the sight is about to cause; the verse prepares for the women's eager speeches in the last four verses.
2531.event: Women gather in the evening, bewildered, to see the procession.

2532.reading: Women with nail-marked sandal-paste on their breasts, their eyes burning and darkening at those who look at them, hold their wreathed hair aside with one hand and fill the street like lamps lit in the middle of the night.
2532.nuance: The hostile figure of Death eating life, borrowed for their glance, turns an angry eye into an erotic one, as the Kural does for a woman's eyes.
2532.event: Women crowd the street, lit with jewels.

2533.reading: Women hide their silk and show their jewelled girdles as drinkers hide their cups, and stand eager to give their blue-lily eyes a feast of the sight, like a coral branch hung with honeyed garlands.
2533.event: Women wait with eyes ready for the sight.

2534.reading: The women make room in the street by stepping back, their breasts firm and not sagging, like the wealth of a just ruler that has no free space above and shrinks below, or like a king who will not hear justice.
2534.nuance: The sceptre doctrine is not the subject; it is the measure of a breast's firmness. The line shows a poet could assume a just king and an unjust king as a common yardstick for shape.
2534.event: Women step back and take places along the street.

claims.claim: a king who will not hear justice shrinks and loses what he has, while a just ruler's wealth fills all space

2535.reading: As people honour only the rich, the women give their jewels only to hips and breasts, saying the poor have no kin, and withdraw with waists worn thin into the houses, a pair of big-eyed women among them.
2535.nuance: The world's partiality towards wealth is used as a simile for the way the body's rich parts take the jewels while the waist is neglected.
2535.event: Women return to their houses, leaving the waist unadorned.

claims.claim: people honour those with wealth and abandon the poor as kinless

2536.reading: Ear-rings bright as cloud-lightning, gold ear-leaves and a forehead ornament frame the faces of the full-breasted women, who look like a moon bearing darkness with blue lilies in a pool set in rows above.

2537.reading: With their garlands dragging, wreaths half arranged, honey pouring from gold-edged buds as bees drone, the women stand half hidden, like the crescent-crowned god taking a woman into one half of himself.
2537.nuance: Civakan's own faith is Jain; the simile uses the Saiva Ardhanarisvara figure, a poet's image without doctrinal claim.
2537.event: Women stand half-hidden behind the crowd.

2538.reading: A man hurrying forward with his gold-streaked garland, flower-topped hair and anklets is watched by maidens who, after looking at themselves in mirrors, grow ashamed, put on more adornments, and fail to find a place.
2538.nuance: The hurrying man is probably Civakan himself, but the verse does not name him; the sense of who is seen by whom turns on the unclear subject of போவான்.
2538.event: Maidens look in mirrors, grow ashamed, and put on more jewels, but find no room in the crowd.

2539.reading: Pearls swinging on their breasts, the courtyards before their houses strewn with gold, and the women glowing so that the sight burns the eyes of those who see them, like a desire-creeper flowering all at once and shedding.
2539.event: Women stand blazing with jewels in the courtyards.

2540.reading: Women with nails reddened with lac and fingers glowing, arms perfumed with aloe, stand bending at the waist under their jewels, their eyes looking like carp glancing at the lightning in the cloud.
2540.event: Women stand dressed, waists bent, looking.

2541.reading: Girls with milk still springing from their breasts, as a mango's juice springs from a broken unripe fruit, stand with narrowed painted eyes, not looking, bent like a wishing-tree branch heavy with fruit.
2541.nuance: The verse's picture of milk springing from the girls' breasts is obscure in line 1; the sense is of fullness, not nursing in a plot sense.
2541.event: Women stand bent, not looking straight.

2542.reading: With bright ornaments flashing, jasmine garlands slipping from their hair and their full breasts sinking under the load of desire, the women stand wishing that all their births to come be like this, like painted dolls on a wall.
2542.nuance: The wish for all births to be as this one treats rebirth as given and wants to repeat it, not to escape it, the opposite of the work's Jain end in release.
2542.event: Women, overcome by desire, wish for the same lot in every birth.

claims.claim: births recur, and a woman may wish her future births to repeat a present joy

2543.reading: Women with bright garlands and fine peacock-like looks, and young men, are all in confusion together, as if a golden world of nagas had fallen here, blossoming blue lilies and red lotuses in every gate.
2543.event: Women and young men mingle, confused.

2544.reading: With the king who wears a hanging-garland umbrella as the sun, the women's faces open like lotuses in a clear pond four leagues wide, and the great eyes seem like blue lilies dazed in the fortress-city.
2544.nuance: The king as sun making women's faces open is a court image of the king as the one who causes the city to bloom.

2545.reading: Dust raised by men and elephants moving in confusion is laid by the honey-drops from the women's garlands, and the golden city, glittering with jewels, seems to flower like a wishing tree.
2545.event: The women's garland-drops lay the dust of the passing procession.

2546.reading: The women say that Pinaiyanar has gained a daughter's wealth and that they themselves have gained eyes this day, and shower flowers on the spear-wounded hero, wishing him a life long as the sea-girt earth.
2546.nuance: Who Pinaiyanar is - the bride's father or another - the verse does not say; it is a doubtful name for a speaker or object of praise.
2546.event: The women bless Civakan and shower flowers on him as he passes.

2547.reading: The women pour powder over him, bow and drop garlands, throw balls full of sandal water and honey, hurl garlands that are tied into wreaths, and sprinkle scented water as he passes.
2547.event: The women pelt Civakan with powder, balls and garlands as a mark of welcome.

2548.reading: The women say he is Murugan's younger brother, Anangan with five arrows, a lion fed by Kandukkan; they are glad in their hearts, their long eyes fixed on him.
2548.nuance: The comparison with Murugan echoes the kings' battle cry in 812, but then it was fear of the one who beat them; here it is longing.
2548.event: The women name him in praise as Murugan's brother, Kama and a reared lion.

2549.reading: With turbans and silks slipping so they hang as ropes, and flowers and garlands falling, the women speak a flawless desire and beg him with their eyes.
2549.nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to construe: தேசிகம் and பாசம் may name the headdress and ropes of cloth; the begging with the eyes is clear.
2549.event: The women beg Civakan with their eyes, their clothes slipping.

2550.reading: After seeing the garlanded one's looks, they say they have lost their own bloom with their bangles, and live seeing his form, praising the women who were born as women as great.
2550.event: The women declare that they have lost their bloom and bangles, and live by gazing at him.

claims.claim: a woman is great who is born to see such a man, and loses her bloom for desire

links.note: The verse measures a breast's shrinking against a king who will not hear justice; Kural 553 says such a king loses his land day by day.
links.teaches: The poet treats the sceptre's decline as a stock yardstick to measure the shape of a body, so the epic's court ethic works as common knowledge rather than argument.

gains.a: A known doctrine of the king's loss that makes the simile of shrinking legible without explanation.
gains.b: A sign the couplet's rule was assumed outside moral discourse, used even in description of a woman's body.

links.note: The verse says the people honour only the rich and the poor have no kin, using it as a simile; Kural 752 states that everyone scorns the poor and honours the rich.
links.teaches: The Kural states the world's partiality as a fact and the epic applies it as a simile, showing the poet treats it as shared knowledge and as a cost on the neglected waist.

gains.a: A flat statement of the rule that the simile of the neglected waist depends on.
gains.b: A case of the rule seen in an unexpected place, the jewelling of a body, not in money.

links.note: The women speak a desire and beg with their eyes, while Kural 1100 says that when two pairs of eyes agree, mouth-words are of no use.
links.teaches: The Kural's silent agreement of two pairs of eyes needs the other side's glance; the women here ask in words and eyes for what he has not yet answered.

gains.a: A standard that shows the women's begging as one-sided and so not yet the eye-agreement the Kural names.
gains.b: A counter-case where eyes and words both ask, showing the couplet's agreement needs two parties.

links.note: The kings in the battle cried that Civakan's chariot was the peacock and he was Murugan; the women now call him Murugan's younger brother.
links.teaches: The same god-likeness that struck the kings with terror strikes the women with desire, showing the epic fits one figure to two audiences.

links.note: In 473 his foster father Kantukkatan receives him lovingly as if Indra's son had come; here the women call him a lion fed by Kandukkan.
links.teaches: The merchant's rearing, hidden in the early books, is now the credential in the city's praise, showing his birth in a merchant house is part of how he is seen as a king.

links.note: Padumai, after one look at Civakan, lost restraint, bloom and bangles; the women of the city now say they lose their bloom and bangles after seeing him.
links.teaches: What Padumai suffered alone is now the whole city's lot, so his beauty is shown to unsettle a crowd as well as one girl.

source_issues: 2527-2531, 2533-2546 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2538 line 2 போவான் has no named subject; 2541 line 1 and 2549 lines 1-2 are hard to construe.
